children: By Emese Bartha

The U.S. Treasury and the Federal Reserve are increasingly working at cross-purposes, potentially exacerbating bond market volatility, according to Ross Pamphilon, CIO of fixed income at Impax Asset Management.

While the Treasury seeks to lower elevated long-end Treasury yields--which spark concerns over fiscal and debt sustainability--,the Federal Reserve remains focused on steering inflation back to its 2% target by signaling a readiness to raise interest rates if necessary.
Raising interest rates typically causes bond yields to increase, even if this tends to impact shorter-dated yields more than longer-dated yields.
"Treasury and the Fed also now appear to be working somewhat at odds with one another, which is puzzling and is itself a potential source of volatility," he said.

In an attempt to curb the surge in long-end yields, the Treasury recently doubled its long-dated securities buybacks to at least $4 billion per operation, up from $2 billion. The announcement followed the 30-year Treasury yield hitting a 19-year high of 5.337% on Aug. 18, Tradeweb data showed.

The market delivered a swift verdict on the buyback announcement, reversing the initial rally in just one day. Yields then declined again but have picked up since, with thirty-year yields creeping back up to last trade at 5.259%.

However, Pamphilon said that the true impact cannot be tested until the increased buyback operations begin this month, when the Treasury could react with determination if long-dated yields continue to rise.
"Our expectation is that if the long end tests the recent highs again, we see larger and more frequent operations, explicit use of the cash balance and a bills weighted refunding," Pamphilon said.
On Wednesday, the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.818%, the highest since November 2023, according to Tradeweb.

The Treasury has tried to establish a floor under the bond market via a visible strike to suppress short-term volatility, he said. That leaves the burden of intervention lying squarely with the Treasury, not with the central bank. Investors could look to test the Treasury's resolve, he said.
"We expect the market to test it. That is the trade we would expect the bond vigilantes to focus on in the fourth quarter."

Pamphilon said analysis of inflation-adjusted yields suggests that investors in long-dated bonds aren't overly concerned about long-term inflation risks. Instead, long-dated yields are being driven higher by concerns about fiscal deficits and debt sustainability.

"Ten-year break-even inflation rates have drifted slightly lower which suggests a moderation in inflation expectations, while real yields have shifted higher. Investors are not asking to be paid for inflation risk, they are asking to be paid for duration risk," he said.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh used last week's Jackson Hole symposium to reinforce his commitment to the 2% inflation target, suggesting that the central bank would act by raising interest rates if necessary.
Pamphilon believes Warsh has limited scope to influence moves in 30-year Treasury yields. The short end of the Treasury yield curve remains "reasonably well anchored," however.

Warsh has expressly avoided giving forward guidance on interest rates and didn't provide any signals on what the Fed will do at its Sept. 16 meeting. However, his hawkish tone "clearly increases the odds of a hike," Pamphilon said.
Money markets currently price in a 65% probability of a rate hike in September, up from 35% before Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, according to LSEG data.
Key U.S. data releases, including jobs and inflation figures, will take on added importance as a result and could intensify bond-market volatility, he said.
"That transfers the burden of price discovery to the market, which means more volatility around each inflation and payroll prints, not less," Pamphilon said.
Impax Asset Management expects it is more likely that the Fed will leave interest rates on hold for now.
"September is a genuine coin flip, and the labor data is the obstacle, so December looks the more probable date to us," he said.
Impax Asset Management managed $30.9 billion in assets as of June 30, 2026.
